Project Name - Employee Mental Health Survey Dataset¶

Project Type - EDA¶

Contribution - Individual¶

* Summary of the project *¶

The main purpose of EDA was to understand the dataset, check its quality, and find important patterns. The Workplace Mental Health Survey Dataset contains 1,259 records and 27 columns. It includes information about employees, their mental health, workplace conditions, and the support provided by their companies.

First, I checked the structure of the dataset and looked for missing values. Missing values were mainly found in columns such as comments, state, work interference, and self-employed status. I also checked for duplicate records and found no duplicate rows.

Next, I identified data-quality issues. The Age column contained some unrealistic values, including negative and extremely large ages. These were treated as data-entry errors and need to be cleaned before further analysis. I also found inconsistent values in categorical columns such as Gender, which should be standardized.

After cleaning and understanding the data, I analyzed important factors such as family history, treatment, work interference, remote work, mental-health benefits, care options, and anonymity.

Overall, the EDA helped me understand the data better, identify errors and missing values, and discover important relationships between workplace support and employees' mental health treatment.

Problem Statement:¶

Mental health is an important issue in the workplace, but many employees may hesitate to discuss their mental health or seek professional treatment because of fear, lack of awareness, or insufficient workplace support.

The main problem is to understand which workplace and personal factors are related to employees seeking mental-health treatment. Factors such as family history, work interference, availability of mental-health benefits, care options, anonymity, remote work, and employees’ perceptions of workplace consequences may influence their decisions.

This project aims to analyze the Workplace Mental Health Survey Dataset using Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) to identify important patterns and relationships in the data. The analysis will also identify missing values, duplicate records, inconsistent data, and unusual values that may affect the results.

The findings can help organizations understand employees’ mental-health needs and identify areas where workplace support can be improved. Ultimately, the project aims to provide useful insights that can help create a more supportive, aware, and mentally healthy workplace environment.

    'man': 'Male',

    'female': 'Female',
    'woman': 'Female'

# Data cleaning function for free-text gender values
def clean_gender(gender):
    if pd.isna(gender):
        return 'Unknown'
    
    gender_str = str(gender).strip().lower()
    
    # Categorize into major standardized groups
    if gender_str in ['male', 'm', 'male-ish', 'maile', 'cis male', 'mal', 'male (cis)', 'make', 'man', 'msle', 'mail', 'malr', 'cis man']:
        return 'Male'
    elif gender_str in ['female', 'f', 'woman', 'femake', 'cis-female/femme', 'female (cis)', 'femail']:
        return 'Female'
    else:
        return 'Non-Binary / Other'

# Apply categorization
df['Gender_Cleaned'] = df['Gender'].apply(clean_gender)

# Frequency distribution
counts = df['Gender_Cleaned'].value_counts()
percentages = df['Gender_Cleaned'].value_counts(normalize=True) * 100

# Output summary table
gender_summary = pd.DataFrame({'Count': counts, 'Percentage (%)': percentages.round(2)})
print(gender_summary)

# Visualization
plt.figure(figsize=(8, 5))
sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid")
ax = sns.barplot(x=counts.index, y=counts.values, palette='viridis')

plt.title('Gender Distribution', fontsize=14, fontweight='bold')
plt.xlabel('Gender Category', fontsize=12)
plt.ylabel('Count', fontsize=12)

# Annotate values on chart
for p in ax.patches:
    height = p.get_height()
    pct = (height / len(df)) * 100
    ax.annotate(f'{int(height)}\n({pct:.1f}%)',
                (p.get_x() + p.get_width() / 2., height / 2),
                ha='center', va='center', fontsize=10, color='white', fontweight='bold')

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

# Plot dedicated clear chart
plt.figure(figsize=(8, 6))
sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid")

ax = sns.countplot(data=df, x='family_history', hue='treatment', palette=['#3498db', '#e74c3c'])

plt.title('Mental Health Treatment Seeking by Family History', fontsize=14, fontweight='bold', pad=15)
plt.xlabel('Family History of Mental Illness', fontsize=12, labelpad=10)
plt.ylabel('Number of Respondents', fontsize=12)
plt.legend(title='Sought Treatment?', labels=['No', 'Yes'], frameon=True)

# Add value and percentage labels
total_no = len(df[df['family_history'] == 'No'])
total_yes = len(df[df['family_history'] == 'Yes'])

for p in ax.patches:
    height = p.get_height()
    if height > 0:
        # Determine total based on x-location
        x_loc = p.get_x() + p.get_width() / 2.
        group_total = total_no if x_loc < 0.5 else total_yes
        pct = (height / group_total) * 100
        ax.annotate(f'{int(height)}\n({pct:.1f}%)',
                    (x_loc, height / 2),
                    ha='center', va='center', fontsize=11, color='white', fontweight='bold')

plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('family_history_vs_treatment.png')
plt.show()

The Family History vs. Treatment graph is a vital component of this survey analysis because it highlights the strongest individual predictor of whether an employee will seek mental health support.

Employees with a family history of mental illness seek treatment at more than double the rate (74.2%) of those without a family history (35.5%).

The three main reason are:

Higher Awareness & Recognition: Prior exposure to mental health topics in their personal lives makes them more aware of available care options (42.7% know their care options vs. 30.5% without a family history) and better equipped to recognize early symptoms.

Reduced Stigma: Having family members who have managed mental health conditions reduces the personal stigma and fear associated with seeking professional therapy or medical help.

Greater Symptom Impact: Employees with a family history report significantly higher frequencies of mental health interfering with their daily work (91.5% experience work interference vs. 67.9% without a family history), creating an urgent, practical need to seek treatment.

plt.tight_layout()

The Work Interference vs. Treatment graph shows that workplace productivity impacts directly drive employees to seek mental health care:

Reactive Treatment Behavior: Employees primarily seek care only after mental health interferes with their work, rising from 14.1% for "Never" to 85.4% for "Often".

Low Preventive Care: Over 85% of employees who experience no work interference do not seek treatment, highlighting a lack of early preventive support.

Performance Trigger: Severe disruption at work acts as the main catalyst for individuals to pursue medical intervention.

The Remote Work vs. Treatment chart is important because it proves that physical work location is not a key driver of mental health care seeking, showing nearly identical treatment rates between remote (52.7%) and non-remote (49.7%) employees.

Findings

Nearly Equal Treatment Rates: Remote workers seek treatment at 52.7% (198 out of 376), while non-remote workers seek treatment at 49.7% (439 out of 883).

Negligible Impact: The minor 3.0% difference indicates that work location (remote vs. office) is not a significant factor in driving mental health care decisions.

Balanced Splitting: Both groups are split almost evenly (50/50) between those who seek treatment and those who do not.

import pandas as pd

for p in ax.patches:
    height = int(p.get_height())
    if height > 0:
        ax.annotate(f'{height}',

This chart demonstrates that employee awareness of mental health benefits directly drives care-seeking behavior, while uncertainty creates a significant barrier to treatment.

Key Findings

Coverage Increases Utilization: Employees who know their company offers mental health benefits seek treatment at the highest rate (63.9%).

Uncertainty Suppresses Action: Employees who do not know if benefits exist have the lowest treatment rate (37.0%), with 63.0% not seeking care.

Significant Awareness Deficit: Nearly one-third of all surveyed employees (408 out of 1,259) are completely unaware of whether their employer provides mental health coverage.

Importance of the Chart

This chart highlights employee awareness of corporate care options as a primary operational leverage point, showing that clear communication directly removes friction to seeking mental health support.

Key Findings

Awareness Drives Care: Employees who clearly know their workplace care options seek treatment at the highest rate (69.1%).

Ambiguity Inhibits Action: Employees who are "Not sure" of their care options have the lowest treatment rate (39.3%), with 60.7% avoiding care.

Widespread Knowledge Gap: More than 65% of respondents (819 out of 1,259) either do not know or are unsure about the mental health care options provided by their employer.

Key Findings Higher Treatment Rates in Larger Companies: Employees in mid-to-large companies (>25 employees) seek treatment at higher rates (52.3%–55.0%) compared to small businesses (44.8%–45.7%).

Small Business Barrier: Small companies (1–25 employees) show the lowest treatment rates (~45%), likely due to a lack of formal benefits or concerns over privacy in tight-knit teams.

Infrastructure Threshold: Treatment rates cross into the majority (>50%) once company size exceeds 25 employees.

correlation heatmap between workplace survey vs treatment seeking¶

In [44]:
# Encode key categorical columns for correlation analysis
df_encoded = pd.DataFrame({
    'treatment': df['treatment'].map({'Yes': 1, 'No': 0}),
    'work_interfere': df['work_interfere'].map({'Never': 0, 'Rarely': 1, 'Sometimes': 2, 'Often': 3}),
    'family_history': df['family_history'].map({'Yes': 1, 'No': 0}),
    'care_options': df['care_options'].map({'Yes': 1, 'No': 0, 'Not sure': -1}),
    'benefits': df['benefits'].map({'Yes': 1, 'No': 0, "Don't know": -1}),
    'anonymity': df['anonymity'].map({'Yes': 1, 'No': 0, "Don't know": -1}),
    'no_employees': df['no_employees'].map({'1-5': 1, '6-25': 2, '26-100': 3, '101-500': 4, '501-1000': 5, 'More than 1000': 6}),
    'consequence': df['mental_health_consequence'].map({'Yes': 1, 'Maybe': 0.5, 'No': 0}),
    'remote_work': df['remote_work'].map({'Yes': 1, 'No': 0})
})

# Compute Pearson correlation matrix
corr = df_encoded.corr()

# Setup heatmap visual styling
plt.figure(figsize=(9, 7))
sns.set_theme(style="white")

# Mask upper triangle for cleaner matrix display
mask = np.triu(np.ones_like(corr, dtype=bool))

sns.heatmap(
    corr,
    mask=mask,
    annot=True,
    fmt=".2f",
    cmap="coolwarm",
    vmax=0.5,
    vmin=-0.2,
    center=0,
    square=True,
    linewidths=.8,
    cbar_kws={"shrink": .8}
)

plt.title('Correlation Matrix: Survey Features vs. Treatment Seeking', fontsize=13, fontweight='bold', pad=15)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Importance of the Chart

This heatmap quantifies linear relationships across all encoded workplace and personal factors, identifying the single strongest drivers of mental health treatment seeking.

Key Findings

Primary Drivers: work_interfere (+0.42) and family_history (+0.38) exhibit the strongest correlation with seeking treatment, indicating personal necessity and genetic predisposition are the strongest motivators.

Organizational Support: Workplace features like care_options (+0.25) and benefits (+0.22) show moderate positive correlations, proving that employer-provided resources directly enable access.

Negative Impact of Stigma: Perceived workplace consequence (-0.12) is inversely correlated with treatment seeking and privacy protection (anonymity), showing fear of negative outcomes deters employee action.

Negligible Impact: Factors such as remote_work (+0.02) and company size (no_employees, +0.08) show minimal direct linear correlation with treatment seeking on their own.

A pair plot visualizes pairwise relationships and single-variable distributions across all numerical and ordinal features in the dataset, segmented by mental health treatment status (Yes vs. No).

Dataset Feature Insights

Age: Normally distributed around 30–35 years across both groups, showing that age alone does not strongly differentiate treatment seekers.

Work Interference: Displays the strongest distributional shift on the diagonal KDE plots; higher interference levels (2 = Sometimes, 3 = Often) strongly concentrate in the Yes treatment class.

Family History: Creates a distinct bimodal separation where respondents with a family history (1) heavily align with seeking treatment.

Benefits & Care Options: Density peaks align at higher values (1 = Yes), showing that employees who know their company provides care options and benefits are significantly more likely to seek care.

Company Size: Uniform distribution across company size buckets (1–6), confirming that company size acts as an enabling context (providing benefits) rather than a direct independent predictor.

Suggestions:¶

Based on the EDA and visualization insights from the dataset, here are strategic, data-driven solutions to improve employee mental health support and increase treatment access:

Key Recommendations

Target High-Risk Triggers: Integrate early intervention resources for employees experiencing daily work friction, as Work Interference (+0.42) is the strongest indicator of treatment need. Implement workload rebalancing and mental health leave policies without performance penalties.

Proactive Screening & Family Support: Develop voluntary, confidential mental health screening programs. Since Family History (+0.38 correlation) is a major driver, ensure health coverage extends comprehensive care to dependents and family counseling services.

Bridge the Care & Benefits Awareness Gap: Enhance internal communication and onboarding regarding company health plans. Increasing awareness of Care Options (+0.25) and Benefits (+0.22) directly correlates with higher treatment utilization.

Eliminate Workplace Stigma & Perceived Consequences: Address negative stigma directly. Negative perceived workplace Consequences (-0.12 correlation) deters employees from seeking help. Establish clear, non-retaliation policies and promote leadership-led mental health awareness campaigns.

Support Small Businesses & Micro-Teams: Provide small businesses (1–25 employees) with subsidized access to shared HR platforms, external Employee Assistance Programs (EAPs), and anonymous third-party mental health apps to overcome the lower treatment rates (~45%) seen in smaller organizations.
